analysis.one_liner: Limits mandatory overtime for nurses at Medicare-participating hospitals and clinics, with retaliation protections and fines.
analysis.headline: Banned mandatory overtime for nurses in Medicare-participating facilities, but it never got a House vote after being referred to committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop hospitals and other Medicare providers from forcing nurses to work beyond their scheduled shift — no more than 12 hours in 24 or 80 hours in 14 days — except during a declared emergency. It also would bar hospitals from punishing nurses who refuse or report excessive overtime, set fines up to $10,000 per violation, and require HHS to study safe maximum work-hour standards for nurses.
analysis.who_benefits: Nurses in hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and surgical centers, who would gain the right to refuse forced overtime without retaliation — and patients, since research cited in the bill links fatigued nurses to higher error rates.

how_it_helps.text: Bars Medicare providers from requiring nurses to work beyond 12 hours in a 24-hour period or 80 hours in a 14-day period, except during a declared emergency.
Prohibits retaliation against nurses who refuse mandatory overtime, report violations, or cooperate in investigations, including reporting them to state licensing boards.
Allows fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with harsher penalties for repeat offenders, and requires HHS to publish violators' names online.
Directs HHS to study and recommend maximum safe work-hour standards for nurses.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and other Medicare-participating providers, which would lose the ability to use mandatory overtime as a staffing tool and could face fines or remediation plans for violations.

drawbacks.text: The exemptions are narrow: the emergency exception excludes routine understaffing, so facilities facing chronic nurse shortages could struggle to cover shifts without mandating overtime.
Enforcement relies on the HHS Secretary investigating complaints and imposing penalties — no automatic oversight or immediate penalty for first violations.
The bill does not require hospitals to hire more nurses, so facilities could still rely on voluntary overtime or scheduling pressure to cover staffing gaps.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a documented safety problem — nurses forced into long shifts, with higher error rates — at the cost of scheduling flexibility for hospitals. The emergency carve-out and voluntary-overtime allowance temper the burden on providers, but enforcement would depend entirely on HHS follow-through.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, never received a markup or floor vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 3, 2007 by Rep. Pete Stark (D-CA) with 86 cosponsors (81 D, 5 R), including Reps. LaTourette and Schakowsky.
Referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and their health subcommittees; no further action followed.
The bill never received a committee markup or floor vote and expired with the end of the 110th Congress in January 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and other Medicare providers that rely on mandatory overtime as a staffing model kept that option, and nurses gained no federal protection against forced overtime.
